s06 — can you filter your way out of reference bias? (chr19, SNP-only)

gwct

08/11/2026 10:57 EDT

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr)
source("analyses/lib/design.r")   # bartheme(), corecol(); knit from the project root

1 Question & design

Can standard hard filters recover the divergence lost to reference bias — or do they only manage false positives? A common reflex is to blame low recall on lenient calling and reach for quality/depth/mapping-quality filters. But a filter can only ever remove calls, so it can raise precision, never recall. This section makes that concrete, and turns up a sharper point: some filters actively amplify reference bias.

  • Data (no new compute). The raw single-shot (iteration 1) caller VCFs, calls.norm, homogeneous divergence D ∈ {0.02…0.10}, 30×, seed 42 — the caller output already exists. Each VCF is read once (bcftools query) and every threshold is swept in memory (analyses/s06-filtering/scripts/filter_sweep.py). SNP filtering uses s01 (SNP-only); indel filtering uses s02 (SNP + indel), scored separately by variant type.
  • Filter axes, one at a time: QUAL (variant quality, column 6); DP (per-sample depth, FMT/DP); MQ (RMS mapping quality — INFO/MQ for gatk & bcftools, INFO/MQM for freebayes). Keep calls with axis ≥ threshold.
  • Metrics (per filtered call set): recall = hom-alt calls matching a truth 1|1 site / number of truth 1|1 sites (the divergence-recovery / reference-bias axis); precision = calls matching any truth SNP site / calls passing the filter. threshold = 0 is unfiltered, so recall(0) is the ceiling and reference bias is 1 − recall(0).
  • Single-shot only. This asks what filtering the caller’s output does; the iterative interaction (filtering during iteration) is deferred — it would need re-running iteration.
prep <- function(path) read_csv(path) %>%
  mutate(caller = factor(caller, levels = c("gatk", "bcftools", "freebayes")),
         axis   = factor(axis, levels = c("QUAL", "DP", "MQ")),
         divergence = factor(divergence))
# SNP filtering on s01 (SNP-only); indel filtering on s02 (SNP + indel)
df <- prep("analyses/s06-filtering/results/s06-filter-sweep.csv") %>% filter(vtype == "snp")
di <- prep("analyses/s06-filtering/results/s06-filter-sweep-s02.csv") %>% filter(vtype == "indel")
dcols <- corecol(pal = "wilke", numcol = length(levels(df$divergence)))

2 Recall is set by divergence, not the filter (SNPs)

Recall of true divergence against each filter threshold. Within a caller, the curves are stacked by divergence and essentially flat in the filter — the ceiling is set by how diverged the genome is (reference bias), and no threshold lifts it. The exception is downward: past a point, filtering starts deleting real calls.

ggplot(df, aes(threshold, recall, color = divergence)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_grid(axis ~ caller, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = dcols, name = "divergence") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "filter threshold (keep calls with axis ≥ threshold)", y = "recall of true divergence") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Interpretation.

  • QUAL: recall is flat across the whole range — the lost variants are not low-quality calls sitting in the VCF, they are absent (never emitted). gatk is perfectly flat; bcftools/ freebayes lose a point or two only at extreme QUAL.
  • DP: a mild, steady recall cost with no compensating benefit — depth filtering removes real low-coverage calls.
  • MQ — the cautionary one: at high divergence, an aggressive MQ cut collapses recall (freebayes drops from 0.98 to 0.62 at MQ ≥ 60, D = 0.10). This is reference bias amplified: the diverged reads legitimately carry lower mapping quality (more mismatches), so an MQ filter preferentially deletes exactly the variants we are trying to recover.

3 Filtering buys precision — mainly for the over-caller (SNPs)

The same sweep, for precision. Filtering’s real value is on the false-positive side, and it is concentrated in the one caller that over-calls.

ggplot(df, aes(threshold, precision, color = divergence)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_grid(axis ~ caller, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = dcols, name = "divergence") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "filter threshold (keep calls with axis ≥ threshold)", y = "precision") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

# the classic view: recall vs precision as QUAL sweeps (each point a threshold)
ggplot(df %>% filter(axis == "QUAL"), aes(recall, precision, color = divergence)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~caller, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = dcols, name = "divergence") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "recall of true divergence", y = "precision",
       title = "Precision–recall as QUAL sweeps (each point a threshold)") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Interpretation. gatk and bcftools are already ~99–100 % precise — filtering does nothing useful, it can only trade away recall. freebayes over-calls (precision ~0.91–0.94 unfiltered), and a light QUAL ≥ 20 cut recovers it to ~0.95–0.97 at negligible recall cost — a real, worthwhile gain. But in the PR view the motion is vertical (precision up) with almost no horizontal travel (recall fixed): filtering moves you up the precision axis, never right along recall.

4 And with indels: filtering fails on both axes

Repeating the sweep on indels (s02, where the truth and callers carry indels) sharpens the message — for indels, filtering helps on neither recall nor precision.

ggplot(di, aes(threshold, recall, color = divergence)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_grid(axis ~ caller, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = dcols, name = "divergence") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "filter threshold (keep calls with axis ≥ threshold)",
       y = "recall of true indel divergence", title = "Indels — recall") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

ggplot(di, aes(threshold, precision, color = divergence)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_grid(axis ~ caller, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = dcols, name = "divergence") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "filter threshold (keep calls with axis ≥ threshold)",
       y = "precision", title = "Indels — precision") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Interpretation.

  • Recall — same story, sometimes worse. No filter recovers indel divergence (the losses are un-emitted, as for SNPs). gatk is flat; bcftools is actively harmed — it already calls few indels at divergence (it collapses on them, per s02), so a QUAL cut drops its indel recall further (0.24 → 0.14 at D = 0.06). MQ again collapses recall at high divergence for the same reason as SNPs (diverged reads carry lower MQ).
  • Precision — filtering can’t fix the over-caller here. For SNPs, a light QUAL cut rescued freebayes’ precision. For indels it does not: freebayes’ precision is stuck near 0.55 even at QUAL ≥ 100 (≈ 251 k false indels remain at D = 0.10). Its complex/multiallelic FP floor is quality-inseparable — the spurious indels carry the same QUAL as the real ones, so no threshold distinguishes them. The one place filtering bought precision for SNPs, it fails for indels.

So the reflex “just filter harder” is even weaker for indels: it can’t recover the lost ones, and it can’t clean up the false ones.

5 Summary

  • You cannot filter your way out of reference bias. Recall of true divergence is set by the divergence itself (the reference-bias floor), not by the filter — because the lost variants are un-emitted (mapping-limited or never assembled; see s05’s mapping-vs-calling split), not low-quality entries a threshold could keep or drop.
  • Filtering buys precision, and only where a caller over-calls — and only for SNPs. freebayes gains a few points from a light QUAL cut on SNPs; gatk and bcftools are already near-perfectly precise and gain nothing. For indels the precision buy disappears: freebayes’ complex/ multiallelic FP floor is quality-inseparable (precision stuck ~0.55 at any QUAL), and bcftools barely calls indels at all, so filtering only removes more of the few it has.
  • Some filters make it worse. Depth filtering costs recall for no precision benefit, and aggressive mapping-quality filtering amplifies reference bias at high divergence — the diverged reads have lower MQ by construction, so an MQ cut deletes the very variants of interest. This is a direct consequence of the mechanism: reference bias penalizes diverged reads at the mapping step, and an MQ filter penalizes them again.
  • Implication for practice: filtering is for precision/FP control, not for recovering divergence. The recall problem is upstream (mapping + assembly), which is exactly what iterative mapping addresses and a filter cannot.

Data table + dictionary in results/s06-filter-sweep.csv. Single seed (42); s01 showed aggregate recall is near-deterministic across seeds. Iteration-1 (single-shot) raw caller calls.
